title: The Friday Night Protests That Reshaped Civic Participation in Japan
content:
For decades, public protest was something many people in Japan preferred to avoid. However, the anti-nuclear movement that emerged after the Fukushima nuclear disaster changed both who participated in protests and how people were mobilised.

Beginning in March 2012, thousands of people started gathering outside the Prime Minister’s residence in Tokyo to oppose the restart of nuclear power plants. The movement was led by the Metropolitan Coalition Against Nukes (MCAN), a network of 13 small activist groups and independent volunteers campaigning for a phase-out of nuclear power in Japan.

Families with children, students, and many first-time protesters became the face of the movement. At its peak in June 2012, following the government’s decision to restart the Ōi nuclear reactors, participation surged dramatically. On 29 June, an estimated 200,000 people, according to the organisers, gathered around the Prime Minister’s residence, making it one of the largest protest movements Japan had seen in decades. The demonstrations continued almost every Friday for nearly a decade.

title: The Power of the Plenum: Leaderless Student Organising in Serbian and Croatian Student Movements
content:
Explore how leaderless, direct-democratic plenums have worked across student movements from Serbia’s 2026 student blockades to Croatia’s 2009 free-education occupation.

Plenums are open, non-hierarchical discussion and decision-making assemblies where every participant holds an equal voice, enabling movements to make decisions collectively without permanent leaders.

Plenums were used by students in Serbia in 2026, building on precedents such as the 2009 protests in Croatia, when students at the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences in Zagreb staged a monthlong occupation. Below is a collection of guides and articles about this decision making model.

If you have practical guides, reflections, or case studies on plenums to suggest please contact us.

A plenum-type gathering is a first-aid kit for patchwork democracy, rooted in the belief that political change from below is possible. – Suzana Ignjatovic

title: Telling Stories under Oppression: The Power of Textiles in Chile
content:
A powerful illustration of how stories can be told in empowering and engaging ways are arpilleras. Arpilleras are three-dimensional, hand-sewn appliquéd tapestries that “tell a story with each stitch”. They originated in Chile as a medium for women, generally working collectively, to denounce the human rights abuses and repression of the Pinochet dictatorship in Chile.

They have since been used to capture the first-person, lived experience of individuals and communities around the world, in response to war and conflict, and a wide range of other forms of oppression and social injustice.

title: Climate Justice and Community Resilience: Mutual Aid, Organising and Disaster Recovery
content:
The resources on this page have been collated by the Commons librarians to support community leaders, organisers and others building resilience and readiness for climate impacts, emergencies and natural disasters.

As the climate crisis escalates more and more extreme weather events are occurring, with big impacts on people and the environment. How communities prepare for these events can make a crucial difference.

On this page we have gathered links to resources in the following areas:

  • Organising: An approach to social change which involves recruiting community members, developing leaders, identifying issues, taking collective action and building and using power for positive outcomes.
  • Mutual Aid: Sharing resources and care at the grassroots level, not waiting for interventions from the state or corporations.
  • Resilience: Building the capacity of individuals, organisations and communities to respond to, and recover from, crisis.
  • Just Recovery: An approach to disaster recovery which centres social justice, addressing power relationships and systemic harms.
  • Collaboration: Ways organisations, communities and government agencies can work together to prepare, respond and recover.

Do you know of a useful guide, template, checklist or other resource for community resilience, emergency preparedness or disaster recovery? We would love to hear about it. title: Hanoi 2015: The City Conceded on Trees, Not on Accountability
content:
The Tree Hugs movement won the argument over trees and lost the argument over accountability. Its petition to Hanoi’s People’s Committee made three demands: stop the felling, open up the decision, and hold officials to account. The first was met within four days. The other two never were. That gap is the lesson.

The movement began with a dismissal. On 17 March 2015, a Hanoi propaganda official was asked whether residents had been consulted about plans to fell 6,700 street trees. There was no need, he replied. Within days, tens of thousands of Hanoians had answered him on Facebook.

No single organisation led the response. It was a loose network of three Facebook groups, drawing mostly young people and women.

No single organisation led the response. It was a loose network of three Facebook groups, drawing mostly young people and women.

The plan was approved in late 2013 without public notice. It would replace 6,708 trees on 190 streets for about US$3.4 million. Officials called it landscaping. Residents saw healthy, century old trees, many planted under French rule, falling within days in a city that shelters under their shade.

title: After School MeToo: Political Mamas’ Fight for Answers in South Korea
content:
During South Korea’s 2018 School MeToo movement, students publicly reported sexual harassment and assault by teachers. But another question remained: how had schools and education authorities responded?

In 2019, Political Mamas, a South Korean nonprofit founded by mothers, and open to other caregivers, began requesting records from regional education offices and mapping publicly reported allegations.

The campaign aimed to make institutional responses visible, identify gaps in investigations and disciplinary action, and strengthen accountability for student safety.

South Korea’s wider #MeToo movement gained momentum in early 2018 after prosecutor Seo Ji-hyun publicly described sexual harassment she had experienced. One Yonghwa graduate later told WomenNews that seeing Seo and Hollywood actresses speak out had encouraged her to do the same.

title: Small Steps 4 Hannah: How One Family Helped Queensland See Coercive Control
content:
In February 2020, Hannah Clarke and her three children, Aaliyah, Laianah and Trey, were murdered in Brisbane, Queensland, Australia, by the husband she had recently left. Her father, Lloyd Clarke, kept asking how he had missed the signs.

Part of the answer was a term many people did not know yet: coercive control. It means using a pattern of behaviour to dominate a partner, such as cutting her off from family, tracking her, and controlling her money. This abuse often leaves no visible injuries.

Within weeks, Hannah’s parents, Sue and Lloyd Clarke, set up the Small Steps 4 Hannah Foundation. It supports people affected by domestic violence, teaches students, workers and families to spot coercive control, and has pushed the Queensland Government to make it a crime.

This article argues that Small Steps used one family’s story to make hidden abuse visible and help write it into law in 2024. Whether the law brings real safety is still unclear.

In its 2016–17 Annual Report, Queensland’s Domestic and Family Violence Death Review and Advisory Board found signs of coercive control in almost all the deaths it reviewed. Yet services rarely responded unless physical violence was also reported.

title: The Right to Sit: How Kerala’s Women Retail Workers Pushed for Change
content:
The Right to Sit campaign in Kerala organized women textile workers around a simple demand—seating at work—and turned their shared grievances into a 2018 legal amendment mandating seats in shops and commercial establishments.

The following article discusses their campaign and the need for workers to keep organizing and monitoring conditions to defend protections.

For many women working in Kerala’s textile shops in India, sitting down was something they had to fight for. They spent long hours on their feet, and some were not even allowed to lean against a wall. Workers reported knee pain and restrictions on toilet breaks. Some avoided drinking water because their shops lacked toilet facilities.

The Right to Sit movement brought these working conditions into public view.

Organising centred on Kozhikode, with protests also taking place in Thrissur and Alappuzha. Penkoottu, a women’s collective whose name means “women’s nest”, and the Asanghadita Meghala Thozhilali Union (AMTU), a union for workers in the unorganised sector, helped workers organise.

title: Voters repudiated Trump. Grassroots momentum will shape what comes next.
content:
This article was originally published on Waging Nonviolence and Truthout.

The broad strokes of the midterms are clear: a massive repudiation of MAGA’s fascist wave has ended the Trump 2.0 era of congressional complicity with his authoritarian takeover. Trump’s lame duck presidency now begins. 

This lopsided electoral rejection is historically rare: Flipping control of both the House and Senate in a midterm has only occurred three times since World War II (1946, 1994 and 2006). The breakthroughs are astounding: the first Native American female governor and senator, five Black governors, the first majority of Democratic governors in 16 years, and critical downballot wins like the first Democrat to win as Texan oil regulator since 1990 and the first openly transgender state legislator in Alabama.
